query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, degradation at elevated temperatures is primarily governed by the selective oxidation of the reactive solute elements (especially Ti and Al) at manufacturing‐induced defect sites (such as porosity and high-energy grain boundaries). The non‐uniform formation and spallation of these oxide products (e.g., TiO2 and Al2O3) lead to local stress concentrations and crack initiation that ultimately trigger catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured alloy with a mainly single-phase face-centered cubic matrix containing inherent additive manufacturing defects (e.g., residual porosity, heterogeneous grain boundaries) and minimal native oxide content.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled high-temperature environments with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (i.e. switching between oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres) during isothermal holds at 700–900 °C.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 700–900 °C, with gas atmospheres ranging from near-atmospheric (oxidizing) to low oxygen partial pressure (reducing); exposure durations long enough to induce observable oxide scale development and mechanical property degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized sites of high defect density (e.g., residual pores and grain boundary regions) that promote rapid diffusion of oxygen and preferential formation of Ti- and Al-rich oxide phases whose non-uniform growth leads to stress buildup and spallation.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the reactive elements (Ti and Al) preferentially oxidize at defect sites. The resulting oxide scales, due to their non-uniform thickness and mismatched thermal expansion relative to the substrate, generate local tensile stresses that cause spallation. This exposes fresh metal to rapid oxidation, accelerates crack initiation and propagation, and eventually leads to catastrophic failure under mechanical load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, samples will develop thicker, inhomogeneous oxide layers concentrated along defect sites, resulting in a detectable reduction in ductility and premature mechanical failure compared to the baseline. Under reducing conditions, the oxide formation will be significantly suppressed, leading to delayed degradation and improved retention of mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy exhibits a homogeneous fcc microstructure with minimal oxide content and sustained mechanical integrity when not subjected to aggressive oxidizing environments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under thermal exposures between 700 °C and 900 °C and when the oxygen partial pressure is sufficiently high to promote rapid oxidation; deviations from these conditions (e.g., reduced oxygen environment) are expected to slow degradation.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative contribution of manufacturing-induced defects versus intrinsic diffusion kinetics of reactive species. The relative roles of Ti and Al oxidation, as well as potential contributions from other minor elemental effects, require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples. Expose subsets to high-temperature holds (e.g., 800 °C) in controlled atmospheres: one in a strongly oxidizing environment (air or high O2 partial pressure) and another in a reducing environment (low O2 or inert gas with a reducing agent). Use in situ high-temperature microscopy and post-exposure cross-sectional analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS) to measure oxide scale thickness, distribution, and the presence of spallation. Complement these with mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compressive tests) to assess ductility and failure onset.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and homogeneity (via SEM/EDS)
Distribution of oxide phases at defect sites (TEM analysis)
Residual mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility) post-exposure
Crack density and location relative to porosity or grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the oxygen partial pressure fails to produce statistically significant differences in oxide formation patterns and mechanical degradation (i.e., if both oxidizing and reducing conditions yield similar oxide scales and failure modes), then the hypothesis that selective oxidation at defect sites governs the degradation and catastrophic failure will be falsified.
